structures.name: Epiglottis
structures.caption: Leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It folds down over the airway when you swallow.

facts.q: What type of cartilage is the epiglottis?

structures.name: Vestibular folds
structures.caption: The upper pair of folds inside the larynx, also called the false vocal cords. They help protect the airway and do not make sound.

facts.q: What is the other name for the vestibular folds?

structures.name: True vocal cords
structures.caption: The lower pair of folds inside the larynx. Air passing between them makes sound. The opening between them is the rima glottidis.

facts.q: Which pair of folds sits lower in the larynx, vestibular or true vocal?

structures.name: Laryngeal prominence
structures.caption: The midline ridge where the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage meet. Called the Adam's apple.

facts.q: Which cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence?

structures.name: Cricothyroid ligament
structures.caption: Connective tissue between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. Clinical landmark for an emergency airway (cricothyrotomy).

facts.q: Which emergency airway procedure goes through the cricothyroid ligament?

structures.name: Thyroid gland
structures.caption: Butterfly-shaped endocrine gland on the front of the trachea just below the larynx. Two lobes joined by a narrow isthmus. One lobe is shown on this model.

facts.q: What connects the two lobes of the thyroid gland?

structures.name: Tracheal rings
structures.caption: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that keep the trachea open. The open side faces backward, where the trachealis muscle closes the gap.

facts.q: What type of cartilage makes up the tracheal rings?

structures.name: Trachealis
structures.caption: Band of smooth muscle across the back wall of the trachea. It bridges the open ends of the C rings, so the back of the trachea is flat and soft against the esophagus.

facts.q: What type of tissue is the trachealis?

structures.name: Carina
structures.caption: Ridge of cartilage at the point where the trachea splits into the right and left primary bronchi. Its lining is very sensitive, and anything that touches it sets off a strong cough reflex.

facts.q: What reflex is triggered when something touches the carina?

structures.name: Right primary bronchus
structures.caption: Wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left. Inhaled objects usually end up here. Remember the model faces you, so its right side is on your left.

facts.q: Which primary bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical?

structures.name: Left primary bronchus
structures.caption: Narrower, longer, and more horizontal than the right because it passes under the arch of the aorta.

facts.q: Why is the left primary bronchus more horizontal than the right?

structures.name: Secondary (lobar) bronchi
structures.caption: One for each lobe: three on the right, two on the left. On this model they are the pale blue stems that lead to each colored cluster.

facts.q: How many secondary (lobar) bronchi are on the right side?

structures.name: Tertiary (segmental) bronchi
structures.caption: One for each bronchopulmonary segment, about ten per lung. On this model they are the color-coded branches.

facts.q: Each tertiary bronchus supplies one of what?
